articles.title: Drivers showed off their parallel parking chops in Pittsburgh. The winner did it in 6 seconds
articles.summary: Parallel parking is a driving skill that can be hard to master. Dan Leber founded Pittsburgh’s Parallel Parking Championship in 2021. Now hundreds of drivers participate in the low-stakes, silly…

image.caption: Clay Hartley won the 2026 Pittsburgh Parallel Parking Championship. He parked his vehicle in just six seconds impressing the judges. (Submitted by Dan Leber)

blocks.text: As It Happens

Parallel parking is a driving skill that can be hard to master. Dan Leber founded Pittsburgh’s Parallel Parking Championship in 2021. Now hundreds of drivers participate in the low-stakes, silly competition.
Pittsburgh’s Parallel Parking Championship is silly, competitive fun, organizer says
LISTEN | Parallel parking competitions are a thing:
As It Happens5:30Drivers showed off their parallel parking chops in Pittsburgh. The winner did it in 6 seconds
Parallel parking is perhaps among many people’s least favourite part about driving. But Dan Leber loves it.
So much so, that he founded and organized the Pittsburgh Parallel Parking Championship. His first event in 2021 drew around 30 participants. This year, nearly 200 people competed.

The idea of watching other people park might sound mundane, but Leber says it’s more exciting than it seems. At the event, participants drive their vehicles into a parallel-parking space and are assigned points for accuracy, speed, and style.
To make things more interesting, Leber and his wife's vehicles are used as markers for drivers to park between. They've been damaged before, but Leber says he's not precious about it.
Hate parallel parking? Here's how the pros do it
Other cities have got in on the action as well, with competitions taking place in Portland and Philadelphia.
Leber says he’s proud he helped create a low-stakes, but fun way for adults to compete against each other. He spoke to As It Happens host Nil Köksal about why he’s passionate about parallel parking.
Dan, what did Clay Hartley do to make him this year's Pittsburgh parallel parking champ?

He did a great job at parallel parking. The space is 20 feet, I think he parked in six seconds, which is remarkably quick. I feel like it was something like 10 or 12 centimetres to the curb, so it was an impressive job.
I thought I was pretty good, but six seconds is fast. Is that the fastest you've ever seen in all your years doing this?
No, six seconds isn't the fastest. I feel like the fastest is under four or five seconds.

The formula someone told me ages ago when I was first learning to drive made it much easier for me. If you can stay calm and the space is a little bit roomy. Do you have a formula that you tell people who are still nervous?

Not really. If people are interested, I kind of give away the secret to winning the contest, which is you have to be lined up and you get one shot. Like you need to whip the car in there, hope that you're within, say six or seven inches of the curb, and then stop. There are so many people who get close and then they put the car in drive and pull up a foot and try to turn in and it's like you just lost it.

items: Parallel Parking: A Dying Art

blocks.text: You mentioned how long your championship has been around. There are competitors now and I want to read you a quote from a recent article in Rodent Track. “Pittsburgh's championship is arguably the loosest run event, as it falls short of banning back-up cameras and parking sensors.” How do you respond to that description?

I think that's hilarious that you bring that quote up because I saw that. I am so proud that we are the first to do this and it kind of originated in Pittsburgh. It's really fun to see how it evolves in other cities because each competition is different. But truthfully, I totally disagree with that sentiment. One of the comments we get most often is people talking about technology in cars, like self-parking and back-up sensors and cameras, and the reality is, when you've seen 700 nearly cars park and you understand the flow of how that works.

It's so clear that the folks who rely on those car aids they don't do well, they don't win, they don't come in second place. It's because they just don't feel the car well enough to do it quickly enough. Certainly you can park well, but it's not gonna take you to the top. The extra time it would take and the efficiency that we would lose in having to cover cameras and explain to [competitors] turn all the stuff off is not worth it, and the truth is that it just doesn't help you.
It’s not an unfair advantage is what you’re saying. What is it that makes you love parallel parking so much? How do you explain that when people ask you why you would start this in the first place?
I think it's interesting for a couple reasons. First of all, it's so low consequence and it doesn't matter. It’s not whether you're good or not, it has no bearing on anybody as a person.
I don't know. Some people use it as a major point of pride.

Yeah, sure, certain people can. But also it's something that most people do a lot and as an adult, I feel like you are less apt to be involved in sports and competitive things. And it's a really silly competitive thing that I think at an individual level, everybody feels and acknowledges alone in a car when they do it. So the idea of taking it to a place where it's a competition among others is really interesting and fun. And again, it's just silly, it doesn't mean anything.
Any damage done to cars in the course of your six years of this competition?

Yeah, I mean damage is relative. We use my wife and my own car, front and back. Everybody comes in a good spirit and certainly some people go for it and the car has been hit, but not to cause any damage. Actually, this year was probably the wildest example of that. There was some guy in a mid-70s blue eight-foot Ford F-150 that was going for it and he somehow hit the curb and my van at the exact same time, which has never happened before.
And you're OK with that? Damage to your cars?
Yeah, they're not precious. Everything's fine.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Marcus Medford is an award-winning multimedia journalist based in Toronto. He's worked as a digital producer, chase producer and senior writer for CBC. He's also written for CTV News Channel and been a reporter for ByBlacks.com and NewCanadianMedia.ca. His interests include current affairs, politics, soccer and social issues. You can reach him with story ideas at Marcus.Medford-Kerr@cbc.ca.
Interview produced by Kevin Robertson

articles.title: Hacked FBI employee data contains sensitive information about intelligence roles
articles.summary: FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about ‌scores of bureau officials’ job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian…

image.caption: FBI data allegedly hacked by a group known as ShinyHunters contains sensitive information about employees, including job assignments, Reuters has found. (Jenny Kane/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about ‌scores of bureau officials’ job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels and more, Reuters has found.
Reuters has found that data allegedly hacked by ShinyHunters has details about work against China, Russia

FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about ‌scores of bureau officials' job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels and more, Reuters has found.

The 5,000-line spreadsheet — said by the hackers to represent only a small piece of their claimed two- to three-terabyte trove — includes names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers, and emergency contact details for what they claimed were thousands of FBI employees.
It also includes details of assignments to specific field offices and, in some cases, ​to units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security or counterespionage work.

In a statement, the FBI said ​it was aware of "a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information."
The bureau said the cause of the breach was still undetermined, but that it was "actively and aggressively investigating the matter."

The hackers said on Tuesday ​that they had breached the FBI, stealing data on a large number of current and former FBI employees. ShinyHunters said it is holding ⁠the data hostage until the bureau rescinds an ⁠unflattering statement about the group issued in May.
'Foreign intelligence service goldmine'
Former FBI counterintelligence operative Eric O'Neill said the data ‌allegedly stolen by ShinyHunters was "a foreign intelligence service goldmine."
"China would be incredibly interested to know the individuals who are working against it," said O'Neill, who founded the cybersecurity company Nexasure AI after his stint at the bureau.
He predicted that other hostile intelligence services would be eager to get their hands on the data, along with disgruntled extremists in the United States.
"If I were on that list I would be very concerned," he said.

items: ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI, stole employee data

blocks.text: ShinyHunters said in ⁠a statement Wednesday that it was trying to keep the personnel information from circulating widely in the meantime.
"If the 5,000 sample data records leak, it's not because of us," the group said.

Although Reuters has not been able to authenticate the entire spreadsheet, it has been able to individually verify the details of more than 22 people by cross-referencing information in the hacked data ‌with credit records and previous data leaks carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs.
Staffers listed China, Russia roles

Some of the assignment details in the ShinyHunters' data are indistinguishable from what employees themselves might say publicly, noting agents at field offices in Baltimore or Newark, New Jersey, for example. Others referred to publicly known bureau subdivisions such as the Internet Crime Complaint Center or the FBI academy at Quantico in Virginia.
But in some cases, the data referred ​to FBI units or initiatives that were sensitive or whose existence has not previously been disclosed.
The data names 14 staffers focused on China-related matters, including members of the "China criminal enterprise unit," the "China tech transfer analysis unit," and the "China intelligence section."
Online learning platform strikes deal with hackers that targeted schools | Hanomansing Tonight

Nine others ⁠are listed as serving in roles related to Russia, including two in the "Russia Operations Section" and one working on "Russia Critical Infra and Tech Threat." Three people are listed as working in ⁠Iran- or Hezbollah-focused intelligence roles.

Eighteen others are listed as working with "data intercept" or "telecom intercept" technologies, or in the FBI's "clandestine technical operations" unit, or its "covert access section," or in ⁠video, audio ⁠or electronic surveillance roles.
A further 11 FBI staffers are listed ​as working in HUMINT, or human intelligence jobs, including several listed as working in the "Humint program management section."

items: A cyberattack hit universities worldwide, including top Canadian schools. Here's what we know
Telus probes cybersecurity incident that 'ShinyHunters' group claims responsibility for

blocks.text: Trevor Hilligoss, a former army investigator who worked with the FBI, said the information ​tying specific named people to human intelligence work was ⁠particularly troubling.
"You don't have to look far to find examples of undercover agents being harmed when their cover is blown," he said.

Hilligoss, now the chief intelligence officer for cybersecurity company SpyCloud, said his concerns were heightened by the inclusion of emergency contacts — often spouses or children — "who may have less operational security knowledge than their relative that works in a sensitive field."

Reuters could not verify that all the job assignments were authentic or up-to-date, but it was able to match the career details or titles of eight people whose data was leaked to information in court filings, ⁠news articles, or public profiles on LinkedIn or to ‌online posts on sites such as Instagram.

articles.title: Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting
articles.summary: Airspace over the German capital was temporarily closed after a drone was spotted on the runway. Flights have resumed but are experiencing delays.

image.caption: https://gadebate.un.org/enImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Berlin's airport briefly suspended flights on Wednesday evening after a drone sighting, Germany's DPA news agency cited airport and police officials as saying.

A drone was spotted on the Berlin Brandenburg Airport's northern runway at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT). Airspace above the airport was closed minutes later and operations were suspended for at least 45 minutes.
Several flights were diverted to Dresden.
As of 9:05 p.m., airspace was reopened but flights were experiencing delays.
Drone sightings on the rise
Drone sightings have become a common occurrence for airports in Europe, with Berlin's airport recording the highest number of sightings in Germany in the first part of the year.

Some 28 drone sightings were recorded during the first six months, as per figures by the German air traffic control (DFS). In seven of those cases, flight operations at the airport were temporarily suspended.
This is an jump from last year, when eight drones were detected at the airport and its surroundings in the whole of 2025, according to DFS.

articles.title: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation stokes division and sows despair
articles.summary:
Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives

Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their…

blocks.text: Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies.
The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise slamming the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation.
Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago.

The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots.
It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence.

“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.
Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”.
Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats.

“You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says.

Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”.

Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks” this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning. It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption.

The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says.
It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals.

One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic. The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect.

Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”.

Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service.

Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”.

The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns.

One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News. Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts

One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024.

Robert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them. He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather he said Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it.
“What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka.
AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns.

The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models.
The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.

articles.title: Health Canada suspends licence to collect plasma at Winnipeg Grifols location
articles.summary: An embattled for-profit plasma centre in Winnipeg is now officially suspended from collecting the blood component, after Health Canada cited concerns about its "quality management" in the wake of a…

image.caption: The Grifols location at 693 Taylor Ave. in Winnipeg. A Health Canada inspection in June found several deficiencies there. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated

An embattled for-profit plasma centre in Winnipeg is now officially suspended from collecting the blood component, after Health Canada cited concerns about its "quality management" in the wake of a donor's death last year.
Company didn’t effectively implement 'corrective and preventive actions,' agency says

An embattled for-profit plasma centre in Winnipeg is now officially suspended from collecting the blood component, after Health Canada cited concerns about its "quality management system" in the wake of a donor's death last year.
The federal agency suspended Grifols's Taylor Avenue plasma centre licence "effective immediately," the regulator announced in an email Wednesday afternoon.

Advocates have been calling on the federal government to crack down on the company after CBC News reported two people died in the past year after donating plasma at Grifols clinics in Winnipeg, including the Taylor location.
Grifols had already temporarily shut down collection at the rest of its Canadian centres last month, citing "unfounded attention" on paid plasma collection in Canada.

"Grifols had not effectively implemented some corrective and preventive actions and, overall, it failed to demonstrate that the Taylor Avenue site has implemented an effective quality management system," Health Canada said Wednesday.
A spokesperson for the Spain-based company said the licence suspension has no impact on its current operations, since collection had already been paused.
The company is working with Health Canada on a reopening plan for its collection centres, the spokesperson said in an emailed statement sent Wednesday.
As of Sept. 1, the company has acquired full ownership of its Canadian operations, the spokesperson wrote, and since then it has been retraining staff and strengthening its procedures.
Grifols operates 17 centres in Canada that pay people for their plasma, including two in Winnipeg.
The now-suspended Taylor Avenue centre is where Rodiyat Alabede, 22, suffered a fatal cardiac arrest while donating plasma on Oct. 25, 2025.
"A temporary suspension is not enough," said Katherine Lanteigne, an advocate for Alabede and her family. She said she wants to see all Grifols sites across Canada suspended.
"Justice will not be served for Ms. Alabede and blood donors in Canada will not be safe if leadership at Grifols are not held accountable for their egregious safety violations."

items: Private clinic Grifols says it's pausing all plasma collection in Canada

blocks.text: The federal regulator initially inspected the Taylor Avenue site roughly a month after Alabede died and found multiple deficiencies it directed Grifols to fix.
After inspecting it twice more over the summer, Health Canada warned Grifols it could suspend the company's licence if the issues weren't addressed.
Health Canada said it proposed suspending Grifols's licence on Aug. 13 and gave the company "an opportunity to be heard."
That same day, Grifols announced it was pausing plasma collection at all of its Canadian locations. It described the pause as voluntary and proactive.
Before the pause and suspension, virtually all of Grifols's locations were already under the regulator's scrutiny.
After its head office in Oakville, Ont., failed an inspection, Health Canada slapped new terms and conditions on its licence for "recurring, systemic deficiencies" that applied to 16 of its centres.
The Winnipeg Innovation Drive site, officially known as Grifols Canada Plasma II Inc., was left out because it operates under a separate licence.
Health Canada said it will work with Grifols as it tries to restart operations and implement corrective action plans.
"Prior to resuming operations, Health Canada will verify Grifols's compliance with our regulatory requirements and we will not hesitate to take further action if needed," the agency's email said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Michelle Allan is an award-winning investigative journalist based in Winnipeg. She's worked with CBC Thunder Bay, CBC's national investigative unit, CBC Ottawa and ran a pop-up bureau in Kingston, Ont. She won a 2021 Canadian Association of Journalists national award for investigative reporting and was a finalist in 2023 and 2024. You can reach her at michelle.allan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Save the Children officially warned by regulator over staff put at risk in Yemen
articles.summary:
Warning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023

The international aid charity Save the Children has…

blocks.text: The international aid charity Save the Children has been issued with an official regulatory warning over management failures and misconduct that put staff at its Yemen office at serious risk.

The warning concluded a two-year investigation by the Charity Commission for England and Wales into the running of the office after the death of its safety and security director, Hisham al-Hakimi, in October 2023 after he was detained by the Yemeni authorities.

The commission said weak governance meant staff at the Yemen office were not properly safeguarded in response to what it called a “live security concern”, and incidents of poor conduct by staff were not addressed.

The warning letter refers to “substantial policy breaches and a lack of accountability” at the office, and said local charity bosses failed to adequately assess and escalate complaints and reports made by whistleblowers.
An internal Save the Children investigation in 2024 after the death of Al-Hakimi found a “negative working culture” in the Yemen office had left staff “disillusioned and marginalised”.
It apologised to staff after admitting it had let them down by failing to properly appreciate the risks facing them amid the deteriorating security situation in the country.

In a statement to the Guardian, Save the Children International said that since 2024 it had made significant changes under new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve support for staff and rebuild trust. The charity has closed its north Yemen office because of security concerns.

It said despite its best efforts to understand the circumstances around Al-Hakimi’s detention and his death the challenges in Yemen meant it may never know what happened and why. Another Save the Children member of staff is understood to currently be in detention.
The commission’s warning comes amid a growing humanitarian crisis in Yemen, where the charity has been providing emergency medical help, shelter and drinking water to displaced families.

Official warnings are relatively rare, and are issued when the commission decides breaches of trust or mismanagement in a charity put its staff or beneficiaries at risk. They can be issued where charity trustees are deemed to have acted recklessly or without proper care.
The commission ordered Save the Children International to ensure sufficient resources are in place to safeguard and protect staff and other individuals working with the charity.

Stephen Roake, assistant director for high-risk compliance at the commission, said: “It can be incredibly difficult for charities operating in high-risk, volatile environments and we know that circumstances can change rapidly. However, it is for this very reason that trustees must ensure they have sufficient oversight of their overseas operations.”

In a statement, Save the Children International said it had accepted the commission’s findings of serious shortcomings in governance, management, oversight and compliance with policies and procedures in the Yemen office at the time.

Since 2024, it had installed new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve staff support and rebuild trust. It had also introduced detention risk assessments, taken steps to improve incident management procedures, and strengthened crisis management.
It said: “We remain committed to learning from this tragedy and ensuring a safe, supportive environment for our colleagues.

“We will continue to work closely with the Charity Commission to address any outstanding matters, while continuing to support our colleagues in Yemen and deliver for children in extremely challenging contexts.”

Save the Children’s Yemen office warned last week that the country faced a “catastrophic humanitarian situation” as a result of escalating conflict, collapsing health services and outbreaks of disease.
More than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded, and tens of thousands displaced by fighting in recent weeks between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.

articles.title: Where did bats come from? Family tree drawn from huge genetic study
articles.summary: Scientists say they've settled the debate about where bats came from and uncovered what the earliest bats were like. They also believe their new huge study of bat genomes and fossils could help…

image.caption: Diaemus youngi, a bat found in Suriname in South America, is one of the species contributed to the Bat1K project by Burton Lim at the Royal Ontario Museum, who co-authored the new study of bat genomes published Wednesday. (Burton Lim/Royal Ontario Museum)

blocks.text: Science

Scientists say they've settled the debate about where bats came from and uncovered what the earliest bats were like. They also believe their new huge study of bat genomes and fossils could help reveal the secrets behind bats' extraordinary disease-resistance and longevity.
Data could be used to figure out bats' secrets to disease resistance, longevity

Scientists say they've settled the debate about where bats came from and uncovered what early bats were like, thanks to a huge study of genomes from all 21 modern bat families and a comparison to dozens of fossil bats.
The earliest bats most likely evolved in Europe around 65 million years ago, reports the new study published Wednesday in the journal Nature.

Previously, scientists have debated whether they could also have come from Asia, Africa or North America – and fossils were too sparse to answer that question, said Sonja Vernes, senior author of the paper and director of the Bat1K consortium behind the study.

"Because bats are flying … they've been dispersing all over the world and crisscrossing the planet for, you know, millions of years," added Vernes, a professor at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, speaking to CBC News from Cyprus where she is studying tiny bats called Miniopterus in local sea caves.
What the earliest bats were like

The researchers learned more about the earliest bats by sequencing genomes from 103 bat species, analyzing their traits and genes, comparing them to 44 bat fossils and using what Vernes called a "complicated advanced computational method."
They learned ancient bats had 26 chromosomes and first evolved around 65 million years ago, after the dinosaurs died out and many mammals started diversifying.

They developed echolocation early on. The analysis shows that the fossil bat Vielasia, which lived 50 million years ago and has a bone structure that showed it could echolocate, was part of the oldest branch in the bat family tree.
Today, there are 1,500 species of bats around the world, representing about a fifth of living mammal species, and the new family tree shows exactly how their 21 families are related to one another.
Mysteriously long-lived
Now that the data has been made publicly available around the world, Vernes said she is "really excited to see what we can learn from their genomes to apply to human health."

Bat researchers have long wondered why bats are so extraordinarily long-lived for their size (up to 40 years, compared to only a couple for similar-sized animals like mice) and unusually resistant to viral diseases. Studying their genomes could help reveal their secrets.
"Maybe it'll help us produce bat-inspired health-care treatments," Vernes said, although she acknowledged that wouldn't be in the immediate future.

The reason she personally likes bats so much is because they're one of the only mammals where the babies have to learn how to speak from adults. "And so that makes them like humans." Her own research, based largely on pale spear-nosed bats in her lab that are originally from Trinidad and Tobago, is on how bats learn vocal communication.
She and Emma Teeling at University College Dublin decided 10 years ago that they wanted to sequence the genomes of every bat on Earth "because they're such amazing creatures."
"We could harness the power of genomics to understand what makes bats special and what they do for the planet."
How the study was done
They built a collaboration of 600 researchers around the world, including 137 from 64 countries who are co-authors on the new paper, including some Canadians.

They include Burton Lim, assistant curator of mammals at the Royal Ontario Museum, who supplied about a third of the samples for genome testing in the study, mostly species from tropical South America and Southeast Asia that he collected using mist nets hung over rivers and the entrances of caves.
His favourites were sheath-tailed bats of Central and South America, which can adjust the membrane between their hind legs to help them manoeuvre during flight.
They're harder to net because they're high-flying.
"So it took me a while to catch them all," Lim recalled. But in the end, he added 25 or 26 species to the ROM's collection.
Inside Alberta's biggest bat cave
While many bat researchers store their specimens in ethanol, Lim said the ROM puts them straight into liquid nitrogen, which allows the genetic information to be preserved much better.

Lim said bats may get a bad rap, but they do a lot of good for the world, from pollination to seed dispersal to eating crop-damaging insects. A 2024 study even showed when bats decline, human infant mortality increases.

Lim hopes that making so many bat genomes available for research will spur other studies looking at the genetics behind things like echolocation and "find out how the [bats] actually do a lot of this stuff that makes bats unique as far as mammals go."

Similar big genome projects are underway for other species, and had previously been done for primates. University of Montreal anthropology professor Joseph Orkin was part of that study, and has found the primate genome data useful in his own research on lemurs.
He said the bat study "looks really exciting," and such a huge database could provide the backbone for answering big questions about bat evolution.
With files from Rosie Fernandez

articles.title: Milei threatens at UN that Argentina will take ‘matters into our own hands’ on Falklands
articles.summary:
Argentinian president accuses United Nations of being filled with ‘parasites’ in bellicose general assembly speech

Javier Milei has condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take…

blocks.text: Javier Milei has condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.

In a caustic speech at the general assembly in New York, the Argentinian president criticised the UN for being ineffective when it came to the long-running tensions over the British overseas territory in the south Atlantic known in Argentina as the Malvinas.

“An organisation that set out to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way regarding the situation of the Falkland Islands,” Milei said of the UN, adding that Argentina was willing to act unilaterally over recent oil exploration near the territory.
The president criticised the Sea Lion project, a major offshore oil development located in the North Falkland Basin, describing exploitation of the territory’s resources as an “unlawful act”.
The president told the assembly that Argentina would “not remain indifferent to those who exploit resources under illegal foreign occupation”.
“Argentina is not going to sit around waiting for the UN and the international community to live up to their own mandate,” he said. “We’re going to take matters into our own hands.”

Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands. Milei’s government began sanctions proceedings this month against more than 60 companies and people linked to the oil drilling project.

The Falkland Islands government had approved the field development and production plans for the project, which is a joint venture between an Israel-based energy company and a London-listed oil and gas exploration company.

The UN does not officially recognise either British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and 3 Falkland Islanders.

“For us, the Malvinas are a national cause,” Milei told the general assembly. The UN, he said, was a “useless organisation whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of faintly arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”.
after newsletter promotion

“That’s why the Malvinas are not merely an issue between Argentina and the United Kingdom,” he said. “They also raise a question regarding the ability of this organisation to enforce its own resolutions.”
A referendum on the political status of the archipelago was held in the Falkland Islands in 2013. On a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.

Milei told the UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply for the Falkland Islands as “the population was implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”. “We call on the United Kingdom to resume negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute as required by international law,” he said.

Last month, Donald Trump said he was ​reviewing the US’s neutral position on ​the Falklands. The issue was a topic of discussion this week in a first meeting between Trump and the UK’s prime minister, Andy Burnham.

“The ‌clear ⁠position is: we will stand firm in the face of any threats,” Burnham said. “We will defend the ​right of ​the ⁠Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British. I just ​wanted ⁠the president to know directly from me, that’s the clear British ⁠position, ​and he very ​much understood what I was saying.”

articles.title: Trump says Canada is 'destroying itself' with immigration. Ministers say that's bogus
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out at Canadian immigration policies on Wednesday, saying the country is "destroying itself" by allowing "millions" of people into the country without proper…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump again set his sights on Canada on Wednesday, this time focusing on immigration policies. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out at Canadian immigration policies on Wednesday, saying the country is "destroying itself" by allowing "millions" of people into the country without proper security checks — comments federal ministers say are ill-informed and grossly inaccurate.
U.S. president claims 'millions' of migrants are coming in unchecked

In a social media post, Trump claimed that Canada is letting too many people in and those who are coming are "essentially unchecked and unvetted" and that's "causing problems that will soon be too big to handle."

All prospective residents go through a multi-step screening process jointly led by Canada's border, security and intelligence agencies. The number of recent arrivals is far fewer than the "millions" the president cited.
"It is a Liberal takeover that will end very badly," Trump said in his latest broadside against Canada.

After a post-COVID surge in new arrivals, the Liberal government led by Prime Minister Mark Carney has slammed the brakes on immigration, curtailing the number of temporary residents, particularly students. That followed the Trudeau government lowering its immigration targets in the fall of 2024.
According to federal figures compiled by the parliamentary budget officer, the number of permanent residents admitted last year returned to pre-pandemic levels with about 328,000 new additions.
The number of temporary residents has plummeted from a peak of 789,000 newcomers in 2023 to a net loss of 382,000 last year.

Statistics Canada data released on Wednesday shows that population growth is at a decades-low level with a year-over-year increase of 189,425 people. That is the lowest annual population growth since 1944-45, the agency said.
That 0.5 per cent annual growth rate is roughly the same level reported in the U.S. under Trump's leadership, according to U.S. Census Bureau figures.
"Let's put some facts on the table," Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York when asked about Trump's comments.
Minister says immigration increases Canadian prosperity following Trump comments

"Canada has had a revised immigration policy since 2024 and we are certainly ensuring our immigration levels, including temporary foreign workers, are reduced in order to stabilize the supports that are available to all Canadians," Anand said.
She said Canada has deliberately curtailed immigration and restored some "stability" to the system to make more homes and health-care services available to the people who are already here.

Rather than something that is "destroying" Canada, Anand said overall immigration has "led to increased Canadian prosperity, especially from an economic standpoint," but the government recognizes that past immigration levels were too high.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser, who was immigration minister during a period of particularly high migration during and after the pandemic, said Trump's claim that people are coming in unvetted is bogus.
"Obviously that's not an accurate depiction of Canada's immigration system," Fraser said. "We scan for security purposes every application for a person seeking to come into this country."
Still, some advocates in this country have said the government needs to scrutinize incoming foreign students more closely. Some alleged Bishnoi gang members have entered Canada on student permits.
Since the Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed and Trump imposed another round of tariffs that are deeply unpopular stateside, the president has been seized with Canada and its leadership.

On Monday, Trump claimed the U.S. would buy potash from Belarus over Canada, even though the Russian-aligned dictator who runs that country says it has none to sell the Americans. Trump later walked back those comments.
Last week, as Carney signalled he wanted Canada to draw closer to the European Union through an "alliance for the future," Trump dismissed that proposed alignment as "laughable."

And he said Canada has been a "terrible trade partner," even though it was his administration that launched a trade war designed to destroy key sectors of the Canadian economy and seems uninterested in the North American trade deal he negotiated in his first term.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

J.P. Tasker is a journalist in CBC's parliamentary bureau who reports for digital, radio and television. He is also a regular panellist on CBC News Network's Power & Politics. He covers the Conservative Party, Canada-U.S. relations, the Crown in Canada, health policy and the Senate. You can send story ideas and tips to J.P. at jp.tasker@cbc.ca

articles.title: Hudson Williams's girlfriend says Heated Rivalry fans crossing 'huge boundary'
articles.summary: Katelyn Larson, a Vancouver-based tattoo artist, made a rare statement about her relationship with Hudson Williams, calling out Heated Rivalry fans for their parasocial behaviour.

image.caption: Hudson Williams, right, attends the 2026 Vanity Fair Oscar party with girlfriend Katelyn Larson in Los Angeles on March 15, 2026. (Neilson Barnard/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Katelyn Larson, a Vancouver-based tattoo artist, made a rare statement about her relationship with Hudson Williams, calling out Heated Rivalry fans for their parasocial behaviour.
Larson, a Vancouver tattoo artist, says fans are booking appointments to ask 'hugely uncomfortable questions'
Hudson Williams's girlfriend, Katelyn Larson, is drawing a line with Heated Rivalry fans.
Larson, a Vancouver-based tattoo artist, made a rare statement about her relationship with the show's co-star, calling out fans for their parasocial behaviour.
"I didn't ever want to have to say anything about this, but a couple people have crossed some boundaries recently so i've gotta say something real quick," she wrote in a Sept. 22 Instagram story.
The two have been in a relationship for a number of years, before Williams shot to superstardom, alongside Connor Storrie, for his breakout role as Shane Hollander in the hit Crave series.

"Obviously a lot of you have found the [tattoo] studio because of a certain show and that's more than okay!" she said. Larson added that if people are following her or other artists because of a genuine admiration of their art or a desire to get tattoos, they can "go right ahead" and shouldn't "feel weird about that."
But Larson says some fans have been booking appointments at her shop solely to ask "hugely uncomfortable" questions about herself and Williams.
"This is where i draw a very hard line," she wrote.

"Booking an appointment with me or anyone else purely because of the connection to the show crosses a huge boundary. Showing up to your appointment and asking my coworkers any sort of questions about myself or about hudson is hugely uncomfortable for everyone. With peace and love, please stop."
Despite Williams's meteoric fame, the couple has largely kept their relationship out of the spotlight, something Williams has made clear in previous interviews.

items: Hudson Williams, Jacob Tierney reflect on Heated Rivalry fame on the CSA 2026 red carpet
Hudson Williams confronts alleged autograph sellers in Paris
Heated Rivalry stars Hudson Williams and Francois Arnaud denounce hateful comments

blocks.text: “She's not trying to be out there or be really perceived,” Williams told ETalk Canada in March.

Williams shared a peek into their personal life on Valentine's Day with an Instagram story dedicated to her, before posing alongside her at the Vanity Fair Oscar party in March, as well as at the Canadian Screen Awards in May
The cast of Heated Rivalry has previously called out bad behaviour by some of their fans on social media.
Williams's massive fandom was on full display earlier this month in Toronto.
Hudson Williams fans line up for hours at TIFF

Williams made an appearance at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) for a special in-conversation event and the premiere of his next project, Yaga, a sex-fuelled mystery series based on Slavic folklore that starts streaming in October.
Dedicated fans told CBC News they waited nearly 12 hours just to catch a glimpse of the Heated Rivalry star and score a ticket to his premiere.

items: Toronto fans go wild for Hudson Williams. And the cast of his new show goes wild for Canada

blocks.text: "Before Hudson, I don't remember the last breakthrough star we had," one fan told CBC News, sporting a Shane Hollander jersey. "And for it to happen so fast and he's like a huge global phenomenon, the most sought-after this TIFF, you have to support it."
"Hopefully he's not the last one," he added, expressing hope that more homegrown talent will reach this level of stardom.
Williams didn't speak to the press on the red carpet, but Yaga co-star Carrie-Anne Moss was asked if she had any advice for him in terms of handling the intense attention he's gotten this year.
Moss kept her answer simple: "He doesn't need it. He's doing great."
The second season of Heated Rivalry is currently filming in Canada and is expected to premiere in April 2027.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: Harvey Weinstein resentenced to 15 years for sexual assault
articles.summary: The disgraced Hollywood mogul was found guilty of sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley. The man whose case spurred the #MeToo movement awaits a separate sentencing in a…

image.caption: A wheelchair-bound Weinstein appealed for leniency to the Manhattan courtImage: Dean Moses/amNewYork/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Disgraced movie mogul Harvey Weinstein was resentenced on Wednesday to 15 years in prison for sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006.

Once one of Hollywood's most powerful kingpins, churning out hits such as "Pulp Fiction", "Shakespeare in Love" and "Chocolat," Weinstein's fall from grace came when sexual assault allegations compounded against him in 2017, spiraling into Hollywood's #MeToo movement.

Accounts of several women who worked with him across the years showed a pattern of abusing his power in Hollywood and ability to make or break careers to extract sexual favors and sexually assault women.
What do we know about Haley's case?
Weinstein was found guilty of forcibly performing oral sex on Haley in 2006.

The former producer said she had accepted an invitation to his Manhattan apartment when he lunged to kiss her, and though she rebuffed him, he grabbed her and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.
Weinstein was sentenced in 2020 to 23 years for the sexual assault of Haley, but the sentence was overturned in 2024 on appeal. A jury found him guilty again in 2025.
What happened in court?
On Wednesday, a 74-year-old, wheelchair-bound Weinstein made an appeal for leniency, apologizing to those he may have hurt.
"I do have remorse for Miriam Haley's pain, but I have to reiterate my innocence," he told the judge.
Haley stressed the assault was akin to "a life sentence."

"Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," she said.
Prosecutors had sought a 20-year sentence for the disgraced producer, but his lawyers warned that a longer sentence would likely see him die in prison.
Is violence against women an epidemic no one cares about?
What other cases await Weinstein in court?

Weinstein also awaits a resentencing in a separate rape and assault case in California, where he is accused of assaulting an actress in a Los Angeles hotel room in 2013. In June, an appeals court upheld his conviction but scrapped his 16-year prison term.
Meanwhile, prosecutors said they will not pursue a fourth trial in the case of him sexually assaulting actor Jessica Mann.

In May, a New York judge declared a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a verdict. It was the third time Mann had taken the stand against Weinstein and she said she could not bear to testify again.
Another 2020 verdict for Weinstein in the Mann case was overturned due to mishandling of witnesses, and a 2025 case ended in mistrial.
Weinstein's lawyers have called for leniency, arguing their client is in failing health as he battles blood cancer, congestive heart failure and kidney issues.

articles.title: New fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region raises fears of a return to the country's civil war
articles.summary: Fighting in and around Tigray is testing Ethiopia's fragile 2022 peace deal. With old enemies forming new alliances, experts warn that the conflict could enter a dangerous new phase.

image.caption: Alula Aba Nega International Airport in Tigray: flights have been supendendedImage: Liu Fangqiang/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: The fighting reported in and around Ethiopia's northern Tigray region marks more than another episode of tension between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the region's leadership. It raises a fundamental question: What remains of the fragile peace established in 2022 — and where does the conflict go from here?

From 2020 to 2022, Ethiopia was devastated by a civil war between the federal government in Addis Ababa and Tigray's regional leadership. The conflict drew in neighboring regions and foreign troops from Eritrea, leading to a humanitarian crisis that displaced millions and left hundreds of thousands dead.
While a peace agreement halted the worst of the bloodshed in late 2022, it left a lot of the political and territorial disputes unresolved.

DW spoke to witnesses in the towns of Abala and Erebti on the border with Tigray who confirmed that new fighting had taken place there between Tigray forces and Ethiopian federal troops. Humanitarian sources also reported clashes in the area. Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to the cities of Mekelle, Shire and Axum, citing the "current situation in the Tigray region."
Reports that Tigray forces have taken control of airports in the region could not independently be verified by DW.
For Oslo-based peace researcher Kjetil Tronvoll, however, the latest developments represent a decisive escalation.
"I think the war has already begun," Tronvoll told DW.
German security analyst Gerrit Kurtz of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin also sees the developments as a serious escalation.
"This is a step towards a war," he told DW.
Two competing narratives
The two sides are presenting fundamentally different accounts of what triggered the latest escalation.

In a statement issued on September 23, the National Regional Government of Tigray said its forces had been responding defensively to an attack by the federal government. It accused Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of launching a new "genocidal invasion" and said Tigray forces had been ordered to defend the population.

The Tigray government also accused Addis Ababa of carrying out air and drone strikes and artillery attacks in recent months. It said it had previously refrained from responding to what it described as repeated provocations in an effort to de-escalate the situation.

The allegations could not independently be verified. The federal government, meanwhile, has portrayed the developments as part of a broader coordinated threat involving armed groups opposed to the prime minister.
The competing narratives illustrate one of the central problems facing any renewed peace effort: The parties do not even agree on the basic interpretation of the escalation.
A fragile peace under pressure

The current crisis cannot be separated from the shortcomings of the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. The deal ended two years of devastating war between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), but it did not resolve some of the conflict's underlying political and territorial disputes.

Western Tigray remains particularly contentious. The return of hundreds of thousands of displaced people remains unresolved, while questions over Tigray's political representation and its relationship with the federal government continue to fuel tensions.
"The Pretoria agreement stopped the fighting, but it did not resolve the underlying political conflict," Tronvoll says.

At the heart of that conflict is a fundamental disagreement over Ethiopia's political order. The TPLF has traditionally defended a strong federal structure and substantial regional autonomy. Abiy Ahmed's government has pursued a more centralized political model.
The issue is therefore not simply whether individual provisions of the peace agreement are implemented. It is also about competing visions of how Ethiopia should be governed.
Former enemies join forces
The emergence of an alliance of seven armed groups opposing Abiy adds another layer of complexity.

The grouping includes the TPLF, Fano forces from the state of Amhara and the Oromo Liberation Army from another regional state within Ethiopia. Some of these organizations were bitter enemies during the Tigray war. Their decision to cooperate therefore represents a significant political development — but not necessarily a durable alliance.
Kurtz says the alliance has been developing for some time and that some of its leaders have apparently already met.
"It was a very important development," he says. "The alliance has been in the making for a long time."
At the same time, he points to the fundamental differences between its members.
"All the political differences that they have are certainly there to resolve once their overall joint aim is achieved, which is overthrowing the government of Abiy."
Tronvoll similarly describes the cooperation as primarily tactical. The question is whether the groups can turn their shared opposition to Abiy into a lasting political and military strategy.
There is another complicating factor: Eritrea.

The Ethiopian government has accused neighboring Eritrea of supporting the alliance. Eritrea has rejected such allegations. Kurtz says there have been reports of contacts between the armed groups and Eritrea, but stresses that the new alliance itself appears to be a domestic grouping.

The geography of the alliance is another obstacle. Its members operate in different parts of Ethiopia and pursue different political objectives. Coordinating military operations across such distances would be difficult.

blocks.caption: Ethiopian security forces in 2021 after they took control of Amhara city from the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF)Image: Minasse Wondimu Hailu/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Can the escalation still be contained?
The most urgent question is whether the current fighting can still be contained before it develops into another full-scale war.
Kurtz argues that the immediate priority is straightforward: The forces involved in the fighting need to stop.
"Both the Ethiopian armed forces as well as the Tigray security forces are involved in active hostilities right now. So they should stop this," he says.

But bringing the fighting to an end will require more than a ceasefire on the ground. Ethiopia's conflict has become increasingly fragmented. Armed groups are operating not only in Tigray, but also in Amhara and Oromia, two other regional states within Ethiopia. Regional actors such as Eritrea are potentially also playing a role.
The new crisis facing Tigray’s families
Who can mediate?
International actors have repeatedly warned about the risk of renewed conflict. Yet sustained diplomatic engagement has so far failed to produce a new political process.

The United States remains an important actor, according to Kurtz, but he says Washington has not shown sufficient engagement. The African Union, the European Union and other international actors could also play a role.
The challenge is that there is no single actor with enough influence over all the parties.

"It will require a certain coalition of efforts," Kurtz says. He argues that preventing a wider war would require a broader diplomatic push, with international actors dividing responsibilities and coordinating their efforts.

The United Nations General Assembly in New York could provide an opportunity for international leaders to engage directly with the Ethiopian government, he says. But diplomacy would also have to address the armed groups involved in the new alliance.

Tronvoll is similarly critical of the international response so far. He argues that the warning signs had been visible for some time but that international efforts to bring the parties back to negotiations remained limited.
The political problem remains

For the people of Tigray, the stakes are particularly high. The region has yet to recover from the consequences of the 2020-2022 war. Many people remain displaced, infrastructure has been severely damaged and the economic recovery remains fragile.

A return to large-scale war would therefore not simply mean a resumption of an old conflict. It could open a new and potentially broader phase of Ethiopia's wider security crisis, particularly given the simultaneous conflicts in Amhara and Oromia.

The immediate priority is to prevent the latest fighting from developing into a wider war. But any sustainable settlement will have to address the political questions that the 2022 agreement left unresolved.
The key question is therefore not simply whether the war has returned.
It is whether Ethiopia and its international partners can still create enough diplomatic space to prevent the latest escalation from closing the door to a political solution.
Ethiopia's broken Tigray peace deal opens old wounds

articles.title: El Niño-driven heat could cause half a million extra deaths, report says. Here's where
articles.summary: This year's powerful El Niño and the record global heat it's driving, along with severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies, could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by…

image.caption: Wildfires in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, this September are one sign of El Niño-driven weather havoc sweeping the planet. (Regina Safri/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Science·New

This year's powerful El Niño and the record global heat it's driving, along with severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies, could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by the end of February, according to a research report released Wednesday.
Climate change is worsening the impacts of El Niño and leading to extreme weather impacts
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Sep 23, 2026 1:06 PM EDT | Last Updated: 25 minutes ago

The grim warning by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab says that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June and the end of February could be attributed to El Niño, compared with heat deaths expected in a typical year.
The heaviest toll, the group says, is expected in poorer countries already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, partly due to climate change and the fallout of the war in Iran.

Michael Greenstone, a co-founder of the group and the study's co-author, said the heat danger will likely persist beyond February — even though this El Niño is expected to end by then. The fallout of the weather phenomenon could be felt well into next summer, he added.
The research, he said, shows that heat is most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor.

"If you're already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous," he said. Wealthier places, he added, generally have greater access to air conditioning, reliable water supplies and functioning health systems.
I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before
The study combined seasonal temperature forecasts with localized estimates of how high temperatures affect mortality across more than 24,000 regions worldwide.

Researchers estimated the additional heat-related deaths by comparing deaths expected under El Niño-driven high temperatures with deaths expected if temperatures remained similar to what they have been in the last three decades. The projected fatalities are for the entire El Niño period, from June 2026 until the end of February 2027.

items: How many people die from heat-related illnesses? The truth is, we don't actually know

blocks.text: Global South will see more heat-related deaths

The study by Greenstone and his colleagues also warns that the Global South — a term that isn't geographical but a reference to developing countries in general — will bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat.

The researchers behind the report found that the Sahel region in Africa — countries along the semiarid southern fringe of the Sahara Desert — is expected to be the hardest-hit, with about 66,800 additional deaths caused by El Niño-driven heat.

items: Facing a super El Niño, this scientist says we can look to the past for climate solutions

blocks.text: Other major hot spots include South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America, according to the report. The researchers project about 19,400 additional heat-related deaths across the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia, as well as 19,300 in Indonesia, 15,800 in India and 13,300 in Brazil.
Heat warnings, cooling centres needed

With such staggering numbers, there are recommended measures that governments can take, the report says. They include heat-warning systems, cooling centers, hydration stations, protections for outdoor workers, expanded hospital capacity and targeted outreach to elderly people and other vulnerable groups.
The authors also call for what they describe as anticipatory financing, so governments can move resources before dangerous heat peaks.
Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report's projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.
But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans and raising needed funds remains a challenge, he said.
"The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari added.
Climate change amplifies El Niño's record heat
El Niño is a natural climate pattern, but this year's unusually strong event is occurring on a planet already warmed by human-caused climate change, increasing the risks from extreme heat.

items: El Niño is here, and it’s already looking like it could be 'mind-blowing'

blocks.text: The Climate Impact Lab said global land temperatures during this El Niño could be higher by about 1.2 C, producing 44 per cent more extremely hot days than in a typical year. The report said those temperature increases may mirror conditions that climate change could make common some 20 years from now.

That's why this El Niño could offer a preview of what's ahead as the planet continues to warm, the report says. It's also an opportunity for decision-makers "to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives," the authors said.

articles.title: Indigenous lawyer wins lawsuit against firm that led class-action for day school survivors
articles.summary: A Manitoba Indigenous lawyer who filed a lawsuit in 2020 against a firm that represented survivors of federal Indian day schools, alleging she was not compensated for years of her work, has won her…

image.caption: Joan Jack has won her lawsuit against the firm that represented survivors of Indian day schools, alleging she was not compensated for years of her work on the class-action case. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

A Manitoba Indigenous lawyer who filed a lawsuit in 2020 against a firm that represented survivors of federal Indian day schools, alleging she was not compensated for years of her work, has won her court case.
'This is a great portion of my life's work. Of course I want to be paid': Joan Jack
Joan Jack summed up her six-year legal saga with one word, using it several times: vindication.

The Manitoba Indigenous lawyer filed a lawsuit in 2020 against a firm that represented survivors of federal Indian day schools, alleging she had not been compensated for years of her work on the class-action case — a $1.47-billion settlement reached in 2019.

Jack filed the original statement of claim for the Indian day school lawsuit against Canada in 2009. In 2016, multinational law firm Gowling WLG became the court-approved counsel for the historic class-action suit.
The 2019 settlement included $55 million in legal fees for Gowling.
In her 2020 statement of claim against Gowling, Jack alleged the firm promised remuneration for her work in the settlement process. That never happened, her claim alleged.

items: Indigenous lawyer files lawsuit against firm representing day school survivors

blocks.text: "If Gowling had intended to do anything other than what they've done, they would have done that, and they haven't, so I was forced to sue," Jack said in an interview on Tuesday.

In a 46-page decision issued on Aug. 31, 2026, Court of King's Bench Justice Shauna McCarthy ruled in favour of Jack. The damages due from Gowling will be determined at a subsequent hearing, the decision states.

“I feel vindicated for sure. I mean, I've been ridiculed. I've been ostracized. Some pretty important First Nations people have said nasty things about me," said Jack, originally from Berens River First Nation on the eastern shore of Lake Winnipeg who now lives in British Columbia.
"So to have the judge in the Court of King's Bench say, ‘Actually, no, this is wrong, and the only question here is the amount of damages,’ that's great. It's very clear, I wasn't treated properly."
CBC News has reached out to Gowling WLG for comment on the decision but has not yet heard back.

Nearly 200,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit were forced to attend nearly 700 federally operated day schools for more than a century, beginning in the 1920s. They were shut out of the $1.9-billion Indian Residential School Settlement Agreement brokered in 2006.
Unlike residential school survivors, day school students remained in their communities and went home in the evenings, but they suffered similar abuse and faced cultural assimilation.
In her 2020 statement of claim against Gowling, Jack said she was responsible for initiating the original day school student claim, and spent years making sure survivors got justice.

items: Indian day school survivors launch $15B lawsuit
Proposed Indian day school settlement to leave out lawyer who filed lawsuit

blocks.text: The original lead plaintiff, Garry McLean from Lake Manitoba First Nation, retained Jack as his lawyer in 2008, the claim said.
Jack's claim said she worked on the case for the next seven years, knowing it was risky. Her own small firm was bankrupted in the process.
She travelled across the country, connecting with thousands of survivors and created a database of their information. She says that information was essential to the final settlement.
Despite the ruling in her favour, Jack said she expects Gowling "to appeal and keep fighting."
"You don't want to get too excited, like this is a long, long haul. So … don't count your chickens before they're hatched," she said.
But "the win is the win" for now, she added, saying she sent the decision to a friend who is a long-serving lawyer, to get his reaction.
"He texted me back and he said, ‘This is a great day, Joan.’ He used the word that I was feeling — he said ‘you've been vindicated.’ Vindicated, you know?”

items: Children at Lake Manitoba Indian day school were strapped for speaking their language, say former students
Residential schools, day schools, day scholars: what you need to know

blocks.text: Even in the case of an appeal, she's in a strong position, the friend told her.
“If this is somebody senior, who has done a lot of litigation, thinking that I should be happy, I guess I'll be a little bit happy,” Jack said.

"So often, we as First Nations, Indigenous people, were wronged, you know, legally. The Canadian state still determines who is registered as an Indian or not. That's legalized racism. We live in that reality.
"So when … the system that oppresses us works in our favour, it's cause for a little bit of breathing room."

She also FaceTimed her mom in Manitoba with the news. After her mom used the word "vindicated" she said regardless of whether Jack sees any compensation "they don't get to rewrite history. You did what you did."
Jack, though, would prefer to see some money.
"This is a great portion of my life's work. Of course I want to be paid," she said.
“I've told my children I have a will, and if I die before this is settled, you make sure the estate lawyer tells my lawyer on the fee file here to keep fighting."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.
With files from Justin Fiacconi

articles.title: Eviction of 87-year-old woman sparks housing protests in Madrid
articles.summary: Police escorted Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had called home for more than seven decades. The case has reignited debate over Spain's housing crisis, rising rents and protections for…

image.caption: 'I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave,' Maricarmen told reportersImage: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman sparked protests in the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday.
Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her residence on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street, where she had lived for at least 70 years of her life.
"I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave," Maricarmen told reporters as the eviction was being carried out.
Dozens of people protested behind the police cordon, chanting, "Maricarmen, you are not alone" and "Murderers!"

blocks.caption: Dozens of protesters gathered as Maricarmen Abascal was removed from her home.Image: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent.
With only 30 minutes to gather her belongings, Maricarmen was escorted by riot police officers. She was removed from her home on a stretcher and taken to an ambulance.
An 8-year-long battle
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, when a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company has lasted eight years, and this was the fourth attempt to evict her from the home.
The elderly woman's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said that the real estate company had rejected proposals from the legal team as well as requests to postpone her removal from the property.
The company has not made any public statements on the matter.

blocks.caption: The case has highlighted the housing crisis in Spain's major citiesImage: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for Inquilinas de Madrid, a tenants' association that seeks to combat what it describes as the "rental bubble" in the Madrid region, said that Maricarmen was taken by ambulance to a local hospital.
She also announced that a writer, who wishes to remain anonymous, had offered to pay the elderly woman's rent, but the real estate company rejected the proposal.
Spain's housing crisis
Spain remains divided over how to address the worsening housing crisis.

The country's left-wing coalition government has pushed for stronger tenant protections and broader rent controls. However, it argues that as long as Parliament remains divided, it will be difficult to pass such measures.
Meanwhile, Madrid's regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, has favored a more market-oriented approach.
The president of the Community of Madrid, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, is currently embroiled in a controversy related to the purchase of luxury properties valued at €6.3 million ($7.2 million).
