articles.title: Iran’s leader hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.summary:
Masoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ‘ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force’

Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump,…

blocks.text: Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing America as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while also insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.

In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to America.

But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”
On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.

A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.

The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on wining the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway which has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to spike.

He made it clear that Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests Iran will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.

Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating Iran’s former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
He also insisted Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme but did not want to build nuclear weapons.

He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security.
“In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.
Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.

Insisting Iran was the victim of true terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”
The leader’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa.
Ultimately Washington granted the permit, but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.

He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”
Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.

Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.

It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.

The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.

The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.

There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.

Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.

Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace proposes $2.45B for reconstruction in Gaza
articles.summary: The board has noted that the Palestinian enclave needs roughly $35.2 billion for full, medium-term reconstruction. Trump's plan for peace in Gaza has largely stalled since an agreement was reached…

image.caption: Nearly a year after the ceasefire started, Gaza remains largely destroyed, with Israeli attacks still a nearly daily occurrenceImage: Ramadan Abed/REUTERS

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has proposed a six-month plan for the reconstruction and governance of the Palestinian Gaza Strip, costing some $2.45 billion (roughly €2.15 billion).
The plan was unveiled during a meeting on Wednesday.

It involves a 66-project blueprint to kick things off, but acknowledges the enormous hurdles that must be overcome to rebuild the devastated enclave, where last October's ceasefire has only slowed Israeli attacks.
What do we know about the Board of Peace Gaza reconstruction plans?
Former UK prime minister Tony Blair, who serves on the organization's executive board, said that Palestinians in Gaza "don't need a slogan; they need a solution."
The reconstruction and governance projects include estimated spending for:

items: Temporary housing
Rubble removal
Hospital repairs
Economic recovery
Deployment of a multinational security force

blocks.caption: Tony Blair outlined the proposal in a keynote speech in New York CityImage: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The initiatives are all designed to support Trump's 20-point plan to end the war.
"The need is immense," the board said, estimating that full reconstruction will cost roughly $35.2 billion over the medium term and another $71.4 billion in the next decade.

The proposal also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects, as per an Axios report released ahead of the meeting.
Could Trump's Gaza plan cost Palestinians their property?
Where do things stand in Gaza now?
Trump's Gaza peace plan, which ushered in the October 10 ceasefire last year, included:

items: Additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza
The disarmament of the Palestinian militant group Hamas
The arrival of an international peacekeeping force
A new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory's day-to-day business

blocks.text: However, almost a year on, completion of the plan has remained elusive..

blocks.caption: Most Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homesImage: Mohammed Skaik/TheNews2/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Israel still occupies roughly 60% of the territory and regularly carries out deadly attacks it says target Hamas militants. Gaza health authorities say over 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed since the ceasefire. The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed.

Hamas, designated as a terrorist group by several countries, has thus far not given up its weapons, despite on some occasions expressing its readiness to do so. Israel has said it will not withdraw from areas it occupies until the group fully disarms and is removed from the enclave.
Meanwhile, most Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homes, with no international military force or new government materializing.
The Board of Peace's high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, has said that progress relies heavily on Hamas disarming, but he has also called on Israel to scale back its military operations.

articles.title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
articles.summary: the disgraced Hollywood producer is already serving a sentence of 23 years for rape and sexual assault in another case.

blocks.text: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.
In a victim impact statement in court, his accuser, Miriam Haley, said the assault had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".

Weinstein has already spent six years in prison as the cases against him play out, and he has a separate conviction for sex crimes in Los Angeles. He has faced three trials in New York over rape and abuse allegations.

He was originally convicted and sentenced in the Miriam Haley case in 2020. But in 2024, New York's highest court overturned the conviction, ruling Weinstein did not get a fair trial. He was retried and convicted again in the case last year.

Weinstein was a high-flying Hollywood producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, before reports in 2017 detailed allegations of sexual assault against him stretching back decades, sparking the #MeToo movement.

articles.title: Biz groups: Bar political families from government contracts
articles.summary: Business groups are urging the government to strengthen safeguards and enforcement mechanisms under a bill barring families of public officials from securing government contracts.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 12:00am

In a statement yesterday, the Management Association of the Philippines, Institute of Corporate Directors and Justice Reform Initiative pushed for refinements in the proposed Government Contracting and Procurement Integrity Act even as it welcomed the Senate’s approval of the bill.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Business groups are urging the government to strengthen safeguards and enforcement mechanisms under a bill barring families of public officials from securing government contracts.
Senate Bill 1962 was approved on third and final reading earlier this month.

“Family-linked procurement creates inherent conflicts of interest, weakens competitive bidding and undermines public confidence even where transactions are technically compliant. SB 1962 addresses this risk at the source by restricting conflicted relationships rather than relying only on disclosure or after-the-fact enforcement,” the groups said.
Among the refinements being pushed by the groups is to require disclosure of ultimate beneficial owners and allow procurement authorities to look through nominee and layered corporate structures.

articles.title: Camille urges respect for absent senators
articles.summary: Sen. Camille Villar teared up as she rebuked Sen. Erwin Tulfo for citing the plunder charges against their detained colleagues during a debate on the conviction threshold yesterday.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Camille Villar teared up as she rebuked Sen. Erwin Tulfo for citing the plunder charges against their detained colleagues during a debate on the conviction threshold yesterday.
Taking exception to Tulfo’s remarks, Villar appealed to the chamber to maintain decorum and extend courtesy to the absent lawmakers, emphasizing that none of them have been proven guilty in court.
The Villars are facing charges for graft, insider trading and market manipulation, among others. Some of their Senate allies are in jail for plunder or hiding from police.
“We owe our absent colleagues some respect because they haven’t been proven guilty of the charges,” Villar manifested.
“They are not plunderers. They are not thieves,” she claimed.
Tulfo apologized for any offense caused by his remarks but clarified that he explicitly used the phrase “charged with,” rather than calling them convicted criminals.
Four senators are currently unable to participate in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte – two are detained, one is in hiding and another on medical leave abroad.
Sen. Mark Villar backed his sister’s call for civility, urging the tribunal to be mindful of the impact of their words on their peers.

articles.title: Metrobank art awardees turn perspectives into possibilities
articles.summary: Drawing from the world around them and their own experiences, the 2026 Metrobank Art & Design Excellence grand awardees transformed themes of power, perseverance and human connection into compelling…

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Drawing from the world around them and their own experiences, the 2026 Metrobank Art & Design Excellence (MADE) grand awardees transformed themes of power, perseverance and human connection into compelling works that invite audiences to reflect, see familiar realities from different perspectives and consider new possibilities.

‘This year, MADE received over 600 submissions from artists across the country, reflecting the diversity, talent and vitality of the Philippine art community. Their works remind us that Filipino artists continue to engage deeply with the world around them and contribute fresh perspectives to the conversations shaping our society,” said Metrobank Foundation president Philip Francisco Dy.
Through painting, mixed media and sculpture, artists charted their own creative paths, translating their observations and questions into works that speak to the world around them.
Awardees were recognized at the Metropolitan Museum of Manila on Sept. 17, marking the opening of the 2026 MADE exhibition.

Open to the public for free from Sept. 18 to Oct. 18, the exhibition features nearly 100 works from different parts of the country that advanced to the semifinals of the competition, including those of the grand awardees.

The 2026 MADE grand awardees each received P500,000 worth of prizes, comprised of P350,000 in cash and a scholarship of P150,000 to the Eskinita Art Residency Program in 2027, as well as the coveted “More” trophy sculpted this year in copper by renowned artist and 2007 MADE awardee Juan Sajid.
A panel of art practitioners, curators, writers and creative industry leaders chaired by sculptor Reginald Yuson selected the 2026 MADE winners.

Joining Yuson were painter and former MADE awardee Mark Andy Garcia, mixed media artist Ling Quisumbing Ramilo, MADE 2026 exhibition curator and University of the Philippines Diliman Department of Theory associate professor May Lyn Cruz, art writer and De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde Creative Industries Program officer-in-charge Lara Acuin, Vinyl Gallery co-founder and co-director Gaby dela Merced and Cultural Center of the Philippines Visual Arts and Museum Division officer-in-charge Rica Estrada.

articles.title: ‘US call to quit ICC won’t affect Duterte trial’
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s call for countries to leave the International Criminal Court (ICC) would not affect the ongoing trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte, who is facing crimes…

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 12:00am

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on September 16, 2026, during a preparatory session as he faces charges over his “war on drugs,” which killed thousands.
AFP / Pool / Piroschka Van De Wouw

MANILA, Philippines — US President Donald Trump’s call for countries to leave the International Criminal Court (ICC) would not affect the ongoing trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte, who is facing crimes against humanity charges over deaths linked to his drug war, Malacañang said yesterday.
Speaking before the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump described the ICC as “out of control” and “rogue” as he urged countries that are members of the tribunal to quit the institution immediately.
He also vowed not to permit US soldiers to face what he called “show trials” before an “anti-American tribunal.”
Asked to react to the stance of the US, Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Marcos’ position on the ICC had not changed.
Marcos had said it was not yet time for the Philippines to rejoin the ICC.
Meanwhile, Duterte’s defense team has asked the ICC to reject the prosecution’s request to accept the testimony of one of its witnesses.

“While the prosecution asserts that P-1100 (witness) can provide evidence of the DDS (Davao death squad) modus operandi, his evidence shows that he had no personal knowledge of this modus operandi, or the structure, operations, hierarchy or command of any such group,” Defense lawyer Peter Haynes said. – Janvic Mateo

articles.title: House wraps up OP budget talks
articles.summary: The House of Representatives terminated plenary deliberations yesterday on the proposed P10.16-billion budget for the Office of the President (OP) for 2027, along with those of the Presidential…

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 12:00am
Groups call for the abolition of the pork barrel and realignment of confidential and intelligence funds, at the House of Representatives in Quezon City yesterday.
Michael Varcas.

MANILA, Philippines — The House of Representatives terminated plenary deliberations yesterday on the proposed P10.16-billion budget for the Office of the President (OP) for 2027, along with those of the Presidential Communications Office (PCO), Presidential Management Staff (PMS) and the Department of Tourism (DOT).

Rep. Albert Garcia, senior vice chairperson of the House committee on appropriations, described the proposed OP budget as largely an operating budget, with P7.46 billion allotted for maintenance and other operating expenses.
Garcia said that the proposed funding comprises only 0.14 percent of the total P7.2 trillion national budget.

He also noted that the proposed budget is 64.02 percent lower than OP’s P28.03-billion allocation for this year, mainly due to the completion of locally funded projects, particularly those related to the country’s hosting of ASEAN 2026.
Even excluding the ASEAN-related expenses, Garcia said the OP’s regular programs were trimmed by P392.52 million, or 3.75 percent from the previous year.
The House also terminated plenary deliberations on the proposed P2.62-billion budget of the PCO and its attached agencies for 2027.

The budget will support the government’s timely provision of accessible information about government policies, programs and services, even as the agency strengthens its presence across traditional and digital platforms.
The House also approved the proposed P851.39-million budget of the PMS for 2027.
At the same time, the chamber also terminated on Tuesday plenary deliberations on the proposed P5.47-billion budget of the DOT.

“Tourism is an investment that multiplies; the government may provide the first peso but tourism allows that peso to move through our economy,” appropriations vice chairperson Rep. Bernadette Escudero said.
Under the proposed P5.47-billion budget, one billion is allocated for DOT’s global branding campaign while P1.37 billion has been provided for the tourism promotion’s board.
Budget ‘railroad’ hit
The Bagong Alyansang Makabayan denounced what it described as the railroading by the House of Representatives of the budget of the Office of the President.
Bayan secretary general Raymond Palatino criticized the “collusion” of Malacañang and Congress in embedding pork barrel and other items in the P7.2-trillion 2027 General Appropriations Bill.
He said nearly half of President Marcos’ budget is allotted for confidential and intelligence funds which should have warranted scrutiny from lawmakers.
“The hasty approval of the President’s budget is reminiscent of the Marcos dictatorship which reduced Congress into a mere rubber stamp institution,” Palatino said in a statement.
Palatino added more than P107 billion were designated for flood control projects despite irregularities involving infrastructure projects that remain unresolved.
He lamented the inadequate subsidies given to the agriculture, health and education sectors.
“We should make sure that Marcos and his allies are not given new opportunities to legitimize the kickbacks they are getting from pork barrel projects,” he said.

articles.title: AMLC freezes P24.7 billion assets in flood mess
articles.summary: The government, through the Anti-Money Laundering Council, has so far frozen a total of P24.7 billion in assets of alleged corrupt officials linked to the multibillion-peso flood control scam ordered…

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 12:00am
This photo shows the Anti-Money Laundering Council seal.
AMLC website

MANILA, Philippines — The government, through the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), has so far frozen a total of P24.7 billion in assets of alleged corrupt officials linked to the multibillion-peso flood control scam ordered investigated by President Marcos in 2025.

This was revealed during plenary deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget at the House of Representatives, when Rep. Presley de Jesus (Philreca party-list) asked AMLC budget sponsor Rep. Ma. Isabel Sagarbarria how has the agency been faring in its efforts to help recover ill-gotten wealth.

Sagarbarria, of Negros Oriental’s second district, replied that these assets have been “preserved” by the AMLC and that the P24.7-billion figure was as of January this year, and that it might even go up.

From the time the flood control scandal broke out in 2025, the lawmaker disclosed that half or 15 of the 30 freeze orders issued by the Court of Appeals have been tied to corruption cases. They included 14 flood control cases covering about P20.2 billion preserved assets.

In the first half of this year – from January to June – 18 of the 28 civil forfeiture petitions in various courts were also linked to corruption cases, covering around P15.7 billion in preserved assets, Sagarbarria added.
There are also five active freeze orders reaching more than P1 billion, now pending before a regional trial court.

In relation to flood control anomalies, 22 petitions have been filed in courts as of Sept. 16 this year covering about P16 billion in preserved assets. All in all for this year, the courts have issued 106 forfeiture orders covering P2.17 billion in total assets.

Of the amount, an estimated P774 million has been returned to the victims of various crimes, P166 million has been turned over to the national government and P119 million transferred to the Office of the Ombudsman.
The AMLC’s proposed budget for 2027 was not challenged during plenary deliberations.
In late August, the AMLC secured a freeze order against the assets of a lawmaker that it refused to identify, but whose case involved “projects worth billions of pesos.”
“The case arose from investigations by the Office of the Ombudsman and the Bureau of Internal Revenue, as well as a separate administrative inquiry by the House of Representatives,” the AMLC said.
The AMLC said the appellate court “found probable cause that the assets were linked to violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, or Republic Act 3019.”
“In a Resolution dated 25 August 2026, the CA ordered the freezing of the assets of the lawmaker, a construction company linked to the legislator, and other associated individuals,” the AMLC added.

“Although the lawmaker claimed he had divested himself of his interest in the construction business before assuming public office, records showed he continued to receive proceeds from the business while in public office, indicating he continued to exercise control over the construction companies.”

The freeze order covers 55 bank accounts and four insurance policies. The AMLC said it remains steadfast in carrying out its mandate to protect the integrity of the Philippine financial system and uphold the rule of law.

Through close coordination with partner agencies, the AMLC said it would continue to pursue measures authorized under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended, to identify, trace, preserve, and recover assets linked to corruption and other unlawful activities.

articles.title: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'
articles.summary: Masoud Pezeshkian's defiant speech to the UN comes after the US president threatened to "annihilate" Iran if a peace deal is not agreed soon.

blocks.text: Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian has told the UN General Assembly that it will never "bend the knee" after almost seven months of war with the US and Israel, but is ready for a diplomatic solution to the conflict.

Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, Pezeshkian said: "He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying."
He also insisted any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ships and ports.
"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access," he said.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the war in late February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US blockade.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Witkoff said he hoped the discussions – the first since June – would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work.

But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

articles.title: Who is skipping the UN General Assembly — and why
articles.summary: Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, Friedrich Merz, Giorgia Meloni and Mahmoud Abbas are among more than 50 leaders who won't make it to the UN General Assembly. Their reasons range from illness and domestic…

image.caption: Empty seats in the United Nations General Assembly hall. This year many states aren't sending their top representativesImage: Shannon Stapleton/REUTERS

blocks.text: Few world leaders would miss a stage like the United Nations General Assembly. Donald Trump, Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Emmanuel Macron are among those in New York for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly — or UNGA81 for short — where the speeches from the green marble lectern make headlines around the globe.
That makes the no-shows all the more surprising. Here is a look at some of the leaders staying away — and why.
Germany: Friedrich Merz

The German chancellor, in his second year in office, would like to be much more present on the international stage and has described himself as a "foreign-policy chancellor." But domestic politics have been keeping him busy. Three German states held parliamentary elections in September and Friedrich Merz is under more pressure as chancellor and leader of the Christian Democrats (CDU) than ever before. In Saxony-Anhalt and Berlin, the CDU was firmly voted out of office, while in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern it failed to enter the state parliament at all — a first since the founding of the Federal Republic of Germany.
Merz is in crisis-management mode at home and seems to want to prevent his opponents from planning a revolt in his absence. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul will speak in his place.

blocks.caption: Not the time for foreign trips: Chancellor Friedrich MerzImage: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

blocks.text: Italy: Giorgia Meloni

Italy's prime minister is in a considerably stronger position than Merz but has said she needs to deal with domestic matters this week. After the NATO summit in early July, Giorgia Meloni said she had just returned from several international summits and had to tackle various issues, including some pending within Italy. She pointed out that Merz had also been absent in 2025 - she too is sending her foreign minister, Antonio Tajani.

blocks.caption: Keeping her focus on domestic affairs: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia MeloniImage: Stefano Costantino/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Africa: Cyril Ramaphosa

The South African president has also just attended an international summit — the BRICS summit in India. He said he would not attend the UN General Assembly for health reasons: medics advised him to take time to rest and recover. His office did not disclose details about his condition. South Africa will also be represented at the UN lectern by Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.

blocks.caption: Resting after a busy travel schedule: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa (pictured here with Indian Minister Jayant Chaudhary)Image: ANI

blocks.text: Egypt: Abdel Fattah al-Sisi

Along with Africa's largest economy, the second- and third-largest economies on the continent are also not sending their presidents to New York: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is being represented by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly. Al-Sisi's office did not give a reason for his absence. During his first years in office, from 2014 onward, he regularly attended the UN General Assembly. In 2020, the event was held online because of the coronavirus pandemic and the following year it was a hybrid event, to which al-Sisi sent a pre-recorded video message. He has not attended since the General Assembly returned to in-person meetings.

blocks.caption: Another BRICS participant: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi (second from left) is not going to New YorkImage: India's Ministry of External Affairs/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Nigeria: Bola Tinubu

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu is the third influential African leader to miss this year's UN General Assembly. His spokesman was quoted by Nigerian media as saying the West African country would be "fully and effectively represented" by Vice President Kashim Shettima. Tinubu, meanwhile, is on vacation: He spent time in the UK in late August before traveling to France.

blocks.caption: On vacation instead of at the UN: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu (front) with Vice President Kashim ShettimaImage: Mubarak Aliyu

blocks.text: India: Narendra Modi

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is relatively rarely to be seen at UN General Assemblies. He last took the podium in 2021, since when the world's largest democracy has consistently sent Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar instead. According to Indian media outlets, Modi was reportedly listed as a speaker at this year's gathering before his plans changed. Why he decided not to attend is not known.

blocks.caption: Unexplained absence: Indian Prime Minister Narendra ModiImage: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: China: Xi Jinping

Chinese President Xi Jinping's absence is under international scrutiny this year. As this year's "High-Level Week" takes place, Xi will also be in the US but he will not be going to New York. Instead, he will head straight for Washington, some 300 kilometers away, for a full state visit, including a White House gala dinner and a military parade.

Although Beijing has not framed it this way, the timing suggests that Xi is prioritizing great power diplomacy over the United Nations' multilateral forum. Xi and Trump have serious bones of contention, including over trade relations, artificial intelligence and Taiwan's security situation.

blocks.caption: Washington instead of New York: Chinese President Xi JinpingImage: Indian Foreign Ministry/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia: Vladimir Putin

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also rarely stood at the iconic podium so it comes as little surprise that Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will once again speak for Russia this year. Putin ordered this by decree — and didn't offer a reason for his absence.

blocks.caption: Skipping the General Assembly as usual: Russian President Vladimir Putin with Foreign Minister Sergei LavrovImage: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: Palestinian territories: Mahmoud Abbas

Mahmoud Abbashas clocked up far more UNGA experience than any of those listed above. The president of the Palestinian Authority (PA), who has been in office since 2005, was a regular until Donald Trump's second term.
But last year, the Trump administration denied him a diplomatic visa and has done so again this year.

Yet, under the 1947 UN Headquarters Agreement, the United States is committed to facilitating access to UN headquarters for foreign representatives. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, for example, is still due to speak in New York, despite the US having recently bombed Iran.

blocks.caption: President of the Palestinian Authority Mahmoud Abbas appears on a screen at the 80th United Nations General AssemblyImage: Jeenah Moon/REUTERS

blocks.text: In the case of the Palestinians, the US State Department recently said it was extending sanctions "that deny visas to members of the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Palestinian Authority." Abbas plans to address the assembled heads of state and government by video message, as he did last year.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
articles.summary: Poland says the aircraft stayed in its skies for 42 seconds, forcing the Nato member to scramble its fighter jets.

blocks.text: Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.

Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.
It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.
Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.

By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.
Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.
A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said.

"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response".
Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.
Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd".
And earlier this week, Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC that his country had already made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they would "not surrender" if attacked.

Meanwhile in Ukraine, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the border with Poland on 13 September shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line.
Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure".

articles.title: Is it unprofessional to bring iced coffee to a job interview? Gen Z is being dragged for it
articles.summary: The debate has divided the internet and generations, with some saying that bringing a beverage to a job interview projects an unserious attitude, and others defending their right to remain…

image.caption: A file photo of a Dunkin' Donuts iced coffee in Burbank, Calif. There's a debate raging online over whether or not it's unprofessional to bring one of these to a job interview, and it's dividing generations. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canada

The debate has divided the internet and generations, with some saying that bringing a beverage to a job interview projects an unserious attitude, and others defending their right to remain caffeinated.
Some say it projects an unserious attitude. But others defend their right to caffeine
The list of acceptable items to bring to a job interview might include, but isn't limited to: your CV, your portfolio, your winning personality, your best foot forward.

But what about your iced latte? That's the debate currently raging online after a job recruiter recently called out Gen Z for showing up to corporate interviews "with iced coffee, iced latte, in hand" in a now-viral TikTok video.

In the video, which has been viewed more than 420,000 times since it was posted last week, U.S. recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen says she believes showing up with an iced beverage comes across as too casual, "like it's just a stop in your list of errands for the day."
"It looks like you went to Target, then you went to Starbucks and now you’re stopping by your interview before moving on to the next thing," Wehniainen said.
"Don't just waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee. It just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand."
The video has divided generations and the internet, with some agreeing that bringing a beverage to a job interview is unprofessional and others defending their right to remain caffeinated.
"It's not about the f--king coffee,"someone posted on Threads. "It's about reading the room, being able to be part of a community and society, compromise, and tolerate discomfort," they added.
It's about basic etiquette, someone else commented on Reddit.
"Arriving at an interview with a beverage for only yourself would be just as impolite as if the interviewer were drinking coffee but didn’t offer you a beverage," they added.
Conversely, how a company reacts to a beverage is a litmus test, others argued.

"In 2026 being YOU is a competitive advantage, and any environment that tries to micromanage something as small as whether or not you brought coffee to an interview is NOT a place you will thrive," marketing professional Zoë Hartsfield wrote on LinkedIn Tuesday.
"No wonder 58 per cent of Gen Z has a side hustle or runs their own company."
How did the Gen Z job market get so bleak?
Generational divide?

The iced coffee debacle isn't the first time Gen Z has been dragged over etiquette and other so-called soft skills. Last year, the term "Gen Z stare" entered the lexicon, which describes the "blank, expressionless" look that the younger generation gives to older generations, particularly in customer service settings, according to Know Your Meme.

And like the "Gen Z stare," some argue the iced coffee debate touches on deeper issues, like how young adults and teens are coping with the lingering effects of COVID-19 lockdowns while facing the worst youth unemployment rate in decades and having to navigate AI's impact on entry-level jobs and recruitment processes.

items: The 'Gen Z stare' mocks youth for staring into the void, but is anyone laughing?
As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection

blocks.text: Gen Z largely came of age during the isolation of the pandemic, tend to prefer digital communication and report higher rates of anxiety than previous generations. Recent surveys have shown that some managers are hesitant to hire younger workers, citing a lack of soft skills like communication and collaboration.
But is the younger generation really bringing iced coffees into job interviews?
Allison Venditti, a Toronto-based human resources expert, says she can count on one hand the number of times it has happened to her, and that's no different to how often it happened 15 years ago.
"We just have TikTok to hear about it now," Venditti, founder of Moms at Work, an advocacy group for working mothers, told CBC News.
"Most folks, Gen Z or otherwise, take the recruitment process seriously and come well prepared and do a great job."
Is the ‘Gen Z stare’ for real?
Is there a middle ground?
That said, Venditti says she does have some iced coffee horror stories, like the time someone brought one in to an interview and accidentally dumped it all over themselves and their papers.
"We spent about 15 to 30 minutes cleaning it up. We also had to find a new room to do interviews as it was sticky. It was awful for all involved," she said.
But maybe there's a middle ground, others argued.

If you do bring an iced beverage into a job interview, don't swirl it around, slurp, put it on the interviewer's desk or hold it in your right hand, since that will make it wet when you shake hands, says Benjamin Chipman, a branding and marketing specialist based in New York City.

"You maybe have one sip that you get to take throughout the entire interview, because that is your opportunity to think a little bit when they are asking you a question," he said in a video posted to LinkedIn.
Which is better than responding with a Gen Z stare, some might argue.
Regardless, the short answer to whether bringing an iced coffee into an interview is unprofessional, is "yes," Venditti says.
"Would you bring a sandwich? No? Then don't bring that, either."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. articles.title: Could a Left Party government in Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
articles.summary: The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum as a way to solve the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?

image.caption: The Left Party has always supported the grassroots campaign that led to the 2021 referendum to expropriate property giant Deutsche WohnenImage: Paul Zinken/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The socialist Left Party, which won the Berlin election on September 20, was the only major party on the ballot that said it would implement the results of Berlin's 2021 referendum, when 57.6% of Berliners voted to expropriate the apartments owned by real estate companies that own more than 3,000 units.
But the federal government has said they won't let it happen. So is it even possible? And how did we get here? DW explains:

items: What did the Left Party say about expropriation?

blocks.text: The Left Party was one of the main supporters of a successful, years-long grassroots campaign called "Deutsche Wohnen & Co. enteignen," ("Expropriate Deutsche Wohnen").
Deutsche Wohnen is a major property developer that owns over 140,000 units across Germany, and 100,000 in Berlin alone.

The campaign and the Left Party argued that by expropriating this and a handful of other major companies like it, the Berlin government could put some 270,000 apartments in Berlin into public ownership, and make them available at affordable rent prices. Other estimates put the number at around 240,000.
The argument struck a chord, as surveys showed that housing and rent prices were the biggest concerns for Berlin voters in the recent election.
Some 25% of rented property in Berlin is already in public ownership, through state-owned companies like Berlinovo. The expropriation measure would likely push that up to over 30%.
Berlin has space, so why is housing so expensive?

items: The 2021 referendum — what was the question and what came out of it?

blocks.text: The original referendum, held in September 2021, asked Berliners to vote yes or no on a five-point plan:
- Socializing the apartments owned by the major property companies
- Administration of the properties by a public-law entity
- Administration of the properties with participation from both city officials, renters, and local communities
- Ban on any re-privatization
- Compensation for the property companies "significantly below" the market value of the property
The referendum did not oblige the state government — at the time a coalition of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the Greens, and the Left Party — to immediately implement the plan.

Instead, the then-SPD Mayor Franziska Giffey put together a 13-person expert commission, including former justice ministers and constitutional law experts. This was given the task of establishing whether the plan conformed with the German constitution, or Basic Law, and how the compensation could be organized.
In 2023, the commission concluded that expropriation was legal and possible, though budget questions still needed to be clarified.

By then, a new conservative-led government, headed by the Christian Democratic Union's (CDU) Kai Wegner, had been voted into office, and announced that it would not expropriate any real estate companies, regardless of what the commission said. At the same time, it emerged that the Berlin CDU was receiving hundreds of thousands of euros in donations from property companies.

Instead, the government said it would draw up a socialization law that would define the conditions for the socialization of property, while ruling out expropriation. A draft law was completed in December 2025.

The Deutsche Wohnen Enteignen campaign rejected this idea as pointless, and had in the meantime gathered legal experts to draw up its own expropriation and socialization law, and promised to start another campaign to force a referendum to implement that.

items: The legal basis for expropriation: Articles 14 and 15 of the German constitution

blocks.text: The original campaign founded its plan on articles 14 and 15 of the German Basic Law.
Article 14 says that, while the right to property is guaranteed, "expropriation shall only be permissible for the public good."

Article 15 states: "Land, natural resources and means of production may, for the purpose of nationalization, be transferred to public ownership or other forms of public enterprise by a law that determines the nature and extent of compensation."
As far as the campaigners are concerned, the law they have drawn up covers those two bases.

But, while Article 14 is implemented often enough (for example, when the state wants to build a new highway), Article 15 has never been implemented at all. It is new legal territory, and no one is quite sure what would happen if it were tried.

Some legal experts say the plan would contravene European law. Housing companies would almost certainly fight the measure in court and demand more compensation than the government is willing to offer.
Business Beyond: The global housing crisis

items: 'Not happening' — Chancellor Merz vows to prevent expropriation

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the Left Party's election victory immediately by promising to draw up a federal law banning state governments from expropriating property.

"It's not just about banning something here in Berlin," Merz said at a press conference in the aftermath of the Berlin election. "It's about sending a clear message to international investors, which is: There is no expropriation of private property in Germany."

However, it's unclear whether the federal government has the power to impose such a law. Germany's Constitutional Court once ruled that the federal government cannot pass a law simply to prevent a state from governing in the issues it wants.

items: What now?

blocks.text: The Left Party still has to enter into coalition negotiations to form a government in Berlin. Its most likely coalition partners are the SPD and the Greens, and given the opposition from the federal government and the massive controversy over the issue, the expropriation plan could become a major sticking point.

Whatever happens, the Left Party itself acknowledges that expropriation and socialization would take a while to put into practice, and it would be even longer before it had a measurable effect on Berlin's overall rents.
In the meantime, it has drawn up a number of laws that it hopes will tackle the problem more quickly, such as a rent cap.

In any case, Berliners themselves appear to have gone a little cold on the idea. Despite the Left's electoral success, a recent poll by infratest-dimap found that only 37% of Berliners are still in favor of expropriating real estate companies.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: China's 13-year-old swimming star raises questions on child athletes
articles.summary: Three gold medals and three Asian Games records have catapulted China's Yu Zidi, 13, into the sporting spotlight. She is far from the first teen prodigy, but should teens be competing at elite level?

image.caption: Yu Zidi has won three golds and set three Games records at the Asian GamesImage: Wu Zhizun/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: The third Asian Games gold medal looked as convincing as the first two, even if Yu Zidi insisted that: "It didn't feel easy at all. It was quite challenging."

On Wednesday, the 13-year-old Chinese swimmer broke the Games record for the third time to add the women's 400 meter individual medley title to her golds in the 200 meter medley and 200 meter butterfly. The three medals add to a bronze she won last year at the World Championships.

Even two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics, talk is turning to a potential rivalry with Canada's Summer McIntosh, 20, who herself finished fourth in the 2020 Olympics at 14 and won a world title at 15. As well as their remarkable talent, the pair's youth has raised some questions.
"The first reaction you have when you see something like this is you think, wow, there's a big career ahead," three-time open water swimming world champion Leonie Beck, of Germany, told DW.

blocks.caption: Summer McIntosh is the only person to have swum faster than Yu Zidi in the 400 meters individual medleyImage: Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: "But I think maybe this is the problem. People around [the athlete], or maybe the media can create this pressure on a young talent. But just because you're really good and fast at this age, doesn't mean that your whole career will continue like this."
Early success is not always sustained

Beck has already retired from elite competition at 29 and swimming is a sport where athletes often peak early. Katie Ledecky, of the US, and Japan's Kyoko Iwasaki both won Olympic gold at 15 and Japan's Yumeki Kojima, 17, has been a home favorite at the Asian Games, winning a gold and silver in the pool.
While the temptation is to think of Yu as a prodigy, Beck said that to reach the level she has also requires extraordinary dedication and sacrifice.

"My first international competition was in 2011 [at age 14]. At that stage already, I was training eight times a week. You wake up at 5 a.m., by 6 you're in the pool, out at 7:30 so you're in school at 8:00, school until 1, going home, eating, maybe doing some homework, going back in the water training at 3. Then one hour of dry land [training], then in the water again and coming back home at 7 (p.m.). I had this when I was young too."

blocks.caption: Leonie Beck won three world and three European titlesImage: Oliver Weiken/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yu, who was discovered by chance by a swimming coach at a water park aged 6, admitted in an interview with state media Xinhua at an event in China in January that the workload takes its toll.
"Being in class all day and still having to train was really tiring," she said. "Sometimes I was so tired I could fall asleep even while eating."

While, for Beck, the sporting success made such struggles worthwhile, not all athletes who dedicate their childhoods to their sport reach the pinnacle. The German swimmer added that putting educational, physical and mental support structures in place is critical for sports that allow under-18s to compete.
"Sport psychology should start at a really young age because it should be normal, the same as physiotherapists," she said. "Especially at a young age, where sport should be also fun."

World Aquatics rules state that the minimum age for international championships is 14 but exceptions can be made for those fast enough, like Yu. While swimmers peak earlier than athletes in other sports, teenagers at the top level are not so unusual.

In football, Lamine Yamal won the Euros with Spain at 16, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, of India, made his debut in cricket's Indian Premier League at 13 and Nadia Comaneci, of Romania, became the first gymnast to be awarded a perfect 10 in the 1976 Olympics in Montreal aged 14.
Neither are young athletes a modern phenomenon. Dimitrios Loundras remains the youngest ever Olympic medallist, winning a bronze with the Greek gymnastics team in 1896.

While support structures in sport are improving, challenges remain, according to Rosemary Purcell, who played a part in the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) review into youth development ahead of the Paris Olympics in 2024.
"There are pretty stark differences between what we see in the community and in these elite youth athletes," Purcell told DW during those Games.

"Some sports do have a higher rate of eating disorders and body image disturbance in young athletes, but conversely, they may have lower rates of depression and anxiety than we would see in the community."
If you're good enough, you're old enough?
In general, sporting bodies tend to take the approach that if an athlete is good enough, they are old enough. Beck said, allied with the right support, this approach is correct.

"Every athlete has completely different development. Why should you take away the success of a young athlete just because she's young and successful in that age? In my opinion, you should give her the possibility to be successful at that age because maybe, who knows, in a later stage of her career, she will be not that successful. It's not just a solution to say: 'look, you're that age, you're not able to compete.'"

But she also cautioned that because success won't always last, young elite sportspeople should be helped to find a plan away from the pitch, pool or mat, something she struggled somewhat with post Paris 2024.

"You have this idea that, ok, I want to reach the Olympic Games, win this medal. So you have a structure of where to go, what to do. And at one point it's gone and you're like, ‘ok, but now what am I doing with my life? What do I want to reach? What are my goals?'
"It's really, really important that people are starting to think that, 'hey, we are also human beings and you should do something to have a life after the sport because the sport is not endless.'"

articles.title: Former U of Manitoba law dean arrested in France, faces extradition to Canada: police
articles.summary: Jonathan Black-Branch, the disbarred former dean of the University of Manitoba's law school, has been arrested in Europe and is facing extradition back to Canada.

image.caption: Jonathan Black-Branch left his position as the dean of the U of M's faculty of law suddenly in 2020 with no official explanation given. The Law Society of Manitoba disbarred him in 2024. (University of Manitoba)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated
Jonathan Black-Branch, the disbarred former dean of the University of Manitoba's law school, has been arrested in Europe and is facing extradition back to Canada.
Jonathan Black-Branch facing Canada-wide arrest warrant for fraud
Jonathan Black-Branch, the disbarred former dean at the University of Manitoba's law school, has been arrested in Europe and is facing extradition back to Canada.
Winnipeg police spokesperson Const. Stephen Spencer confirmed Wednesday the arrest happened in France and the matter is currently before the French court system.

Police can't say more while the matter is before the courts, he said in an email, but "further information will be provided should the extradition application be successful" and Black-Branch is returned to Winnipeg.
He could not confirm when Black-Branch was arrested.
Black-Branch, who was hired as U of M's law dean in 2016, left his post suddenly in 2020 with no formal explanation given.
Around the same time, an internal investigation by the university, based on a whistleblower complaint, found a senior university employee misspent university funds.

items: Former U of Manitoba law dean disbarred in U.K., still under Canada-wide arrest warrant

blocks.text: In 2023, a months-long law hearing by the Law Society of Manitoba found Black-Branch had committed professional misconduct and misspent more than $600,000.

He spent U of M endowment funds on expensive meals at the members-only Manitoba Club, personal education at Ivy League schools, accommodation, travel and other expenses while he was dean of the U of M's law school, according to the society's decision.
The U of M then asked Winnipeg police to investigate for possible criminal charges.
The law society disbarred Black-Branch in 2024, removed his name from its rolls of barristers and solicitors, and fined him $36,000.

While overseas in August 2020, the University of Southampton, in the U.K., announced Black-Branch as the new head of its law school. Days later, the university changed course and announced it would no longer be hiring him.
Earlier this year, Black-Branch was disbarred for a second time.

The Bar Standards Board for England and Wales barred him from practising law, citing his actions in Manitoba as "blatant and sustained dishonesty," according to the disciplinary decision by the Bar Tribunals and Adjudication Service.
The Canada-wide arrest warrant was issued for Black-Branch on March 30, 2026, on a charge of fraud over $5,000.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 29: Court overturns initial 16-conviction threshold in VP trial
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually…

blocks.text: The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling after some senators became unavailable to participate in the impeachment trial.
On July 6, presiding officer Senator-judge Francis "Chiz" Escudero set the number of votes needed to convict at 16, or two-thirds of all the 24 senators.
Article 11, Section 6 of the Constitution does not state a number and instead reads, "No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.”
The same constitutional provision also states that "The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment."
Those who voted in favor of Tulfo’s motion are:

items: Paolo Benigno "Bam" Aquino IV
JV Ejercito
Sherwin Gatchalian
Risa Hontiveros
Panfilo Lacson
Lito Lapid
Francis Pangilinan
Vicente "Tito" Sotto III
Erwin Tulfo
Raffy Tulfo
Joel Villanueva
Mark Villar
Juan Miguel Zubiri

blocks.text: Of the 13, only Senator Villar is from the Minority bloc.
The lone no vote came from Escudero.
The six minority bloc senators who did not participate in the vote are:

items: Alan Peter Cayetano
Pia Cayetano
Christopher Go
Imee Marcos
Robin Padilla
Camille Villar

blocks.text: Defense team lead counsel Sheila Sison said the Vice President’s camp will exhaust all legal remedies to address the new threshold for conviction, among other things.

"She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available sa ilalim ng ating batas at Konstitusyon na may pagtatangi sa esensya ng isang tunay na malayang, demokratikong institusyon. At karapatan ng bawat mamamayan na madinig sa isang hukuman na walang kinikilingan o kinakatakutan," she added.

(She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available under our law and Constitution, with due regard for the essence of a truly free, democratic institution. And it is the right of every citizen to be heard in an impartial court that fears no one.)
Alan Cayetano attempted to defer the voting, to no avail.
No acquittal by default

Ahead of the vote, House prosecutor Chel Diokno of Akbayan party-list said the threshold must be changed since the Vice President’s case should be decided on merits, not by default or absence of senator-judges.

“Yes, the Constitution deliberately makes conviction harder by imposing the two-thirds requirement. But making it harder is not the same as making it depend on senators who are not judges or who are incapable of acting as judges. That would be tantamount to an acquittal by default, a failure to arrive at the threshold number caused not by the judgment of the incapacitated senators, but by their mere inclusion in the denominator,” Diokno added.
Defense counsel Michael Poa, however, said that the July 6 ruling of Escudero setting 16 votes as the threshold cannot be appealed since it is not provided under Senate impeachment rules.

“Last July 6, 2026, on the very first day of trial, the presiding officer ruled that a voting threshold to convict is 16. At that time, no senator-judge objected. No senator-judge sought reconsideration. No senator-judge appealed. Your Honors, that was over two months ago. There is no supervening event. Our point is, nothing changed between July 6 and today,” Poa said.

Escudero, however, had a rebuttal for Poa by citing the Supreme Court decision in People v. Amigo, GR number 116719, which states that Supreme Court decisions are “not petrified rules grown rigid once pronounced, but may be reconsidered upon further reflection in light of new perspectives.”

“The July ruling issued during an ongoing proceeding is not a final judgment on any Article of Impeachment. It cannot claim greater; therefore, this issue cannot claim greater immutability than the judicial doctrine itself. Where the governing impeachment rules prescribe no period and no final judgment has been rendered, the court remains free to reconsider its interpretation,” Escudero said.

Erwin Tulfo also addressed Poa’s comments that there is no supervening event, citing that their four colleagues being detained due to alleged plunder, being in hiding from authorities and being on leave are something that the court should address as elected representatives of the people.
Camille Villar then appealed to his colleagues not to attack their detained fellow senators, saying that they are not yet convicted of their alleged crimes.
Her take was seconded by his brother, Mark Villar, citing that there should be respect among colleagues.
Erwin Tulfo apologized if his comments offended his colleagues, but he stressed that he never said their colleagues were convicted of crimes.
“What I said was they were charged in court,” Tulfo said.

“Further, the statements were not attacks against our fellow senators but merely confronting the present reality that some senators are physically or legally unable to participate in the impeachment trial. The issue of detained senators is so intertwined in the determination of the denominator,” Tulfo added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Pakistan's jailed former PM Khan's sons told DW the authorities are cracking down ahead of new PTI protests
articles.summary: The sons of jailed Pakistani ex-PM Imran Khan told DW their father is in ill-health while being isolated from family and doctors. Other family members have been detained ahead of a planned opposition…

image.caption: Despite being jailed since 2022, Khan remains a popular political figure in PakistanImage: K.M. Chaudhry/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Family members of Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan are concerned about the 73-year-old's health in a Rawalpindi prison, accusing authorities of preventing him from accessing appropriate medical care.
Khan's London-based sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, told DW they have received "little to no information" about their father's health condition.
"When we last spoke to him on the phone back in March, he said that he had lost 85% of the vision in his right eye and that despite his complaints, it was neglected for months," they said.

The brothers added that their father was being held in a tiny cell and has been allowed outside for only one or two hours a day. They also allege that the elder Khan was kept in isolation from family, lawyers, and a personal physician for 10 months before he was briefly allowed to see two of his sisters.
This comes amid the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party's planned protest march on September 27 to exert pressure on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government for Khan's release.
Sons demand family access and medical care for Khan
Khan's sons are urging authorities to allow their father to receive an independent medical assessment and restore regular access to his family and medical team.

"We are asking the Pakistani authorities to obey the Supreme Court orders immediately and shift our father to Shifa International Hospital so that he can be assessed by independent doctors," they said.
They also called for Khan to be allowed his mandated family visits, phone calls with his sons, and access to a personal physician.

blocks.caption: Pro-Khan protesters clashed with authorities during a 2024 protestImage: ASIF HASSAN/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Khan's sisters detained as PTI plans new protests

Despite being in jail, Khan remains at the center of Pakistan's political confrontation between the PTI and the country's powerful military. He also remains a popular political figure in Pakistan, despite being ousted from office in 2022 in a parliamentary no-confidence vote.
Amid plans for a PTI protest march set for this weekend, Khan's three sisters were detained in the Punjab capital of Lahore on Monday.
The detention orders cited concerns that the sisters were a threat to public safety and maintenance of public order. All three were ordered to be held for 30 days under a public order ordinance.
Khan's sons told DW the arrests were intended to intimidate their family and supporters before the planned protest rally.

"Our family members who have been arbitrarily taken into custody must be released immediately," they said. "The abductions of our family members in the middle of the night, with no reason given, were purely to intimidate them," they added.

Khan was ousted as prime minister in 2022 and jailed the following year on what he says are politically motivated corruption charges. Khan's family members, and his PTI opposition party, have faced an ongoing government crackdown.

blocks.caption: The detention orders for Khan's sisters cited concerns that they were a threat to public safety and maintenance of public orderImage: AAMIR QURESHI/AFP

blocks.text: Pakistan government calls for 'order'
Pakistan's government has rejected the PTI's characterization of the crackdown and says its priority is to maintain public order during the planned protest.
Talal Chaudhary, Pakistan's minister of state for interior, has warned that the government will not tolerate unlawful activity or actions threatening lives and property.
"If you are a peaceful citizen, come to Islamabad from any route, come 100 times," Chaudhary told DW.
"But if you come as terrorists, we will not let you leave," he added.

In 2024, pro-Khan protests on the streets of Islamabad turned violent. Demonstrators breached high security zones and clashes with security forces, leaving six dead. When Khan was first arrested in May 2023, nationwide PTI support rallies also led to violence, with military and government buildings suffering damage. Several people were killed and hundreds injured.
Chaudhary said the government would not tolerate unlawful activity or actions threatening lives and property.
"The right to protest does not give the right to attack," he said.

Authorities have stepped up security preparations in Islamabad and Rawalpindi ahead of the protest, including the deployment of thousands of police personnel and the placement of shipping containers and other barriers at key entry points.
Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war?
Arrests could 'galvanize' PTI supporters
The PTI has said the September 27 protest will demand Khan's release and push for what the opposition describes as respect for constitutional and political rights.

Michael Kugelman, a South Asia analyst at the Washington-based Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, told DW the arrests will likely further energize Khan's supporters ahead of the planned protest.
"The arrests will galvanize what is already an angry and anxious Khan support base," Kugelman said.

The detention of Khan's sisters, who Kugelman said are "prominent advocates" of Khan's cause, has also placed his family increasingly at the center of the confrontation between the government and the PTI.
Khan's base is "concerned about the state of his health, and for his sister to be detained will increase the chance that protesters take to the streets on the 27th," he added.
Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader and close aide to Khan, said the arrests were meant to create fear but will not prevent the party from mobilizing its supporters across the country.
"What they don't realize is all they are doing is creating more hatred for themselves among the public," Bukhari told DW, referring to the government.
Bukhari described the current crackdown as the most severe the PTI has faced. "This crackdown seems the more brutal," he said, adding that the government was acting out of frustration.

"They are fueling a fire that will soon be out of their control," asserted Bukhari. "They can keep attacking us, and we will continue to resist. This protest will go on, and many more after it," he added.

As Pakistan's government is dealing with several challenges, including economic malaise, conflict with the Afghan Taliban, and fallout from the Iran war, further domestic unrest would be an unwelcome complication.
Pakistan: 'Security state' on the rise amid regional tension
